passage: Okay, don't laugh, but there's a boy in the next section who looks at me like I'm made of glass. I'm Gopika. His name is Arnab. He waits by the gate each morning and copies down whatever I say in the canteen queue, and last week he slipped a card into my bag that said I was the most perfect person he knew. Part of me went pink and pleased. Another part felt hot and cornered, like I had to be perfect now. I didn't want to laugh at him or boast to my friends about it. So I found him near the water cooler and said, "Thanks, that was kind. But I'm just a person who forgot her tiffin yesterday. And please don't wait at the gate every day, it makes me nervous." He blushed hard, but he nodded.

qa.q: Where does Arnab wait for Gopika each morning?
What mixed feelings did Gopika have about the card?
qa.a: Flattered and uneasy. Part of her went pink and pleased, and another part felt hot and cornered, as if she had to be perfect now.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that was wise?
qa.a: She thanked Arnab kindly, told him she was just a person, and clearly asked him not to wait at the gate every day.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt when Gopika spoke to him at the water cooler?
qa.a: Embarrassed, since he blushed hard, but he nodded, so he may have understood. Being seen as a person and not an idol can sting a little before it helps.

grounding: Gopika is flattered and uneasy about a boy who idolises her and kindly tells him she is just a person and sets a boundary.

qa.q: What does Kishore feel about Pallavi's notes?
qa.a: He feels flattered but uneasy, since she sees him as perfect when he is just an ordinary person who failed a chemistry test.

qa.q: What is Kishore planning, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To talk to Pallavi normally, thank her kindly, remind her he is ordinary and ask her not to wait outside class, which is kind but sets a boundary.
Pallavi seems to see him as a perfect, cool hero, so she may feel shy and hopeful when she leaves notes and waits near him.

grounding: A teen worshipped from afar feels flattered and uneasy, refuses to use it for power, and plans to be kind and set boundaries.

passage:
For two weeks now, someone had been leaving marigolds in Aparna's cycle basket outside the Government Girls' School. On the third Sunday at the village mela, she saw who: Gopal from the boys' school across the pond, watching her from behind the balloon stall like she was a film heroine.
Her friend Simran giggled. "He's crazy about you. You could make him do anything."
Aparna felt her cheeks warm. It was nice, being looked at like that. It was also uncomfortable. Gopal didn't know that she bit her nails and failed her Sanskrit test.
On Monday, when he appeared near her cycle again, she said calmly, "Gopal, thank you for the flowers. They're pretty. But I'm just an ordinary girl, not someone in a film. Please don't leave them anymore."
Gopal went red, nodded and walked away fast. Aparna felt a pang, but also lighter.

qa.q: Where did Aparna find the marigolds?
qa.a: In her cycle basket outside the Government Girls' School.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she learned it was Gopal?
qa.a: She felt flattered and warm-cheeked but also uncomfortable, because he saw an idealised version of her.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than Simran's suggestion, and why?
qa.a: Aparna thanked Gopal kindly and asked him to stop, rather than using his feelings for power, which respected both of them.

qa.q: How might Gopal feel after Aparna speaks to him?
qa.a: Gopal probably feels embarrassed and disappointed, but she was kind, so he can walk away with his dignity.

grounding: A teen idolised by a boy feels flattered and uneasy, reminds him kindly that she is ordinary, and sets a boundary.
